title: Demonstrate an understanding of good manufacturing practices in food processing

lessons.title: What good manufacturing practice covers
lessons.html:
GMP: the foundation of safe food

Good manufacturing practices (GMP) are the basic operating conditions and procedures that a food plant needs to produce safe, wholesome food consistently. GMP is the foundation on which HACCP and food safety management systems such as those required by retailers are built. In an abattoir, deboning plant or poultry processing plant, GMP touches everything: the building, the equipment, the people, the water, the materials and the records.

Main areas of GMP

AreaExamples
PremisesSmooth, washable walls and floors; proper drainage; separation of clean and dirty areas; adequate lighting and ventilation
EquipmentFood-grade materials such as stainless steel; easy to clean and maintain; calibrated instruments
PersonnelHygiene, protective clothing, health screening, training
SanitationWritten cleaning schedules, approved chemicals, verification of cleanliness
Pest controlProofing of buildings, monitored bait stations, contracted service records
WaterPotable water supply, regular testing, hot water for sterilisers
MaterialsApproved suppliers, inspection of incoming packaging and ingredients
Storage and transportTemperature control, stock rotation, clean vehicles
DocumentationProcedures, records, traceability, recall plans

Why GMP matters

  • Prevents contamination and food-borne illness.
  • Meets legal requirements, such as those under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulations, and the requirements of food safety inspectors.
  • Meets customer and export requirements.
  • Reduces waste, rework and customer complaints.
  • Protects the brand and the jobs of everyone in the plant.

lessons.title: Premises, equipment and hygienic design
lessons.html:
Building and equipment that support hygiene

Plant layout and product flow

A well-designed plant moves product in one direction, from dirty to clean, without crossing back. In an abattoir the flow typically runs from lairage and stunning, through bleeding, skinning or defeathering and evisceration, to inspection, chilling, cutting and dispatch. Inedible material and waste leave by separate routes. Staff entrances, change rooms and hygiene stations are placed so that people pass through hand washing and boot washing before entering production.

Surfaces and structure

  • Floors must be impervious, non-slip, sloped to drains and kept in good repair.
  • Walls should be smooth, light-coloured and washable to a suitable height.
  • Ceilings must not shed flakes, condensation or dirt onto product.
  • Doors should close properly; strip curtains and fly screens must be intact.
  • Lights over product areas should be shatterproof or covered.

Equipment

Equipment that touches food should be made of non-toxic, corrosion-resistant materials like stainless steel or food-grade plastic. Wooden items are generally avoided in production because they absorb moisture and bacteria. Equipment should be easy to take apart and clean, with no hollow spaces or rough welds where residues collect.

Maintenance and calibration

A planned maintenance programme keeps equipment working and prevents physical contamination such as loose bolts or worn blades. After maintenance, the area and equipment must be cleaned before production resumes. Maintenance staff must follow the same hygiene rules as production staff and account for all tools. Thermometers, scales and metal detectors must be calibrated against known standards on a schedule, and the results recorded.

Glass and brittle plastics

Many plants keep a glass and hard plastics register listing every item in production areas. Items are checked regularly. If something breaks, production stops in that area, the product nearby is held and the area is cleaned under supervision.

lessons.title: People, processes and documentation
lessons.html:
GMP in daily operations

Personnel practices

  • Health screening at employment and reporting of illness before shifts.
  • Clean protective clothing issued and laundered by the company where possible; no protective clothing worn outside the plant.
  • Hand washing at the correct times and with the correct technique.
  • No jewellery, eating, smoking or personal items in production.
  • Visitors and contractors follow the same rules and sign in.
  • Ongoing training, with records kept for each employee.

Process controls

  • Temperature control in chillers, freezers and during processing, monitored and recorded.
  • Stock rotation using first expired, first out (FEFO) or first in, first out (FIFO).
  • Segregation of raw and ready-to-eat products, and of condemned or held product, clearly labelled.
  • Allergen control where ingredients such as soya, wheat or milk proteins are used in processed meat products.
  • Foreign body control such as metal detection and knife integrity checks.

Cleaning and sanitation programme

A master sanitation schedule lists what is cleaned, how, how often, with what chemical and by whom. Cleaning is verified by visual inspection before production starts and periodically by swab tests. Chemicals are used at label strength and stored in a separate locked area.

Documentation and traceability

Standard operating procedures describe how tasks are done. Records show they were done. Traceability means you can trace product one step back to its source and one step forward to the customer. Mock recalls test whether the system works. Records must be accurate, completed at the time, and kept for the required period.

The supervisor's role

Supervisors enforce GMP on the floor by leading by example, conducting pre-start inspections, correcting poor practice immediately and respectfully, and escalating problems such as broken equipment or pest activity.

Key points

  • GMP covers premises, equipment, people, sanitation, pests, water, materials, storage and records.
  • Product should flow from dirty to clean areas without crossing back.
  • Equipment must be food-grade, cleanable, maintained and calibrated.
  • Personal hygiene, stock rotation and segregation are daily GMP controls.
  • Traceability allows product to be traced back to its source and forward to the customer.

quiz.question: What is the relationship between GMP and HACCP?

options.text: GMP is the foundation on which HACCP is built
HACCP is only for office work

quiz.question: Which direction should product flow in a well-designed abattoir?

options.text: From dirty to clean areas without crossing back

quiz.question: Why are wooden items generally avoided in production areas?

options.text: They are not available in South Africa

quiz.question: A light cover breaks above a deboning table. What should happen?

options.text: Stop production in the area, hold nearby product and clean under supervision
Move the product to another table and continue
Wait until the end of the week to report it
